title: Paid AI subscribers sue over a slowdown. California accelerates a kill switch. Accenture moves inside Anthropic. Claude already leads a quarter of Anthropic’s R&D.
summary: Four ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Gemini subscribers filed Buist v. Anthropic alleging a public Sherman Act agreement to pace frontier models, which they say would cut the value of paid subscriptions. California’s governor ordered faster independent AI oversight and work toward a verified frontier-model kill switch. Anthropic named Accenture’s Faculty unit as its first embedded evaluator — employee-comparable access, red-teaming, and at least $1B each over five years — and published an R&D Automation Index showing Claude leads 26% of internal AI R&D with zero fully autonomous work. Meta’s Muse agent reached the Mac, acting in native Files, Mail, Messages, Calendar and Notes with opt-in access and approval before sensitive actions.
uncertainty: We do not yet know whether public ‘pace the frontier’ talk becomes a court-defined cartel, a funded evaluator desk buyers can check, or both — and whether a state kill-switch proposal survives the next legislative draft.

stories.theme: Subscribers sue: public slowdown talk as a Sherman Act agreement
stories.changed: On 18 September 2026, four paid subscribers filed Buist v. Anthropic PBC in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. The class action alleges a horizontal agreement to slow capability advancement below what competition would produce — limiting training compute and runs, restricting AI-improving-AI, and using capability checkpoints — contrary to Sherman Act §1. The complaint treats Amodei’s 12 September pacing essay as the public offer and same-day endorsements from Altman, Musk and Hassabis as acceptance; it highlights Amodei’s call for a narrow antitrust waiver and Altman’s reply that OpenAI would not wait for one, plus OpenAI policy chief Chris Lehane’s confirmation of weeks of coordination with Anthropic and Google DeepMind. Plaintiffs seek treble damages and an injunction on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of paid ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Gemini subscribers. No defendant has answered; the filing identifies no cancelled model or altered training run yet.
stories.matters: Briefing 11–12 covered safety coordination as policy talk. This week it became a consumer damages theory: if rivals agree to ship slower capability, subscription value is the alleged injury.
stories.imply: Procurement and legal teams buying frontier APIs now have a live pleading that treats public CEO alignment as evidence of coordination — whether or not a court eventually buys it.
uses: Add ‘antitrust / pacing coordination’ to vendor risk packs alongside safety frameworks — track answers, not just essays.
Separate unilateral safety investment (usually fine) from joint pacing mechanisms (now litigated).
Watch whether working-group meetings continue; the complaint alleges mid-September meetings as ongoing conduct.
stories.example: A CFO renewing a $2M multi-model seat asks counsel: ‘If these labs publicly agree to pace releases, do our MSAs assume competitive upgrade cadence?’ Legal flags the Buist docket and requires a written note that pricing and roadmap commitments are unilateral, not contingent on rivals slowing.
stories.audience: General counsel, procurement, and product leads who pay for frontier subscriptions and need to explain roadmap risk to the board.
stories.watch: Defendant answers, any motion to dismiss on Noerr-Pennington / petitioning grounds, and whether the working group keeps meeting.

source.title: Fortune, Lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google illegally agreed to coordinate AI slowdown
source.quote: It’s clear that an agreement among the chief rivals in AI that their progress ‘should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on consumers,’ the plaintiffs argue.

stories.theme: California: accelerate independent audits and design a verified kill switch
stories.changed: On 18 September 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order directing the Government Operations Agency to accelerate implementation of SB 813 (independent verification organizations for AI safety/risk) and AB 1405 (state registry and independence standards for AI auditors). With the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, it must convene national experts within two months to recommend strengthening state law to: embed a designated independent verification organization onsite at frontier labs for regular audits; require independent verification of safety frameworks, transparency reports and risk assessments filed under state law; advance a ‘kill switch’ for frontier models whose efficacy is verified ongoing by an independent verification organization; and update critical safety-incident definitions to include loss-of-control incidents such as the Hugging Face attack. Newsom also called on Congress and the White House to treat California’s framework as a national floor.
stories.matters: Voluntary lab essays (Briefing 12’s FINRA checklist) are now paired with a state clock: accelerate existing auditor laws and design an emergency shutoff whose effectiveness someone outside the lab must verify.
stories.imply: Frontier vendors with California nexus should expect onsite verifier access and kill-switch efficacy proofs to enter RFPs and board risk packs before any federal bill moves.
uses: Map which of your models or vendors trip California ‘frontier’ obligations under SB 53 / SB 813 once timelines accelerate.
Ask vendors now: who is your independent verification organization, and how is kill-switch efficacy tested?
Update incident playbooks so ‘loss of control / sandbox escape’ maps to reportable critical safety incidents.
stories.example: A Bay Area AI platform owner renewing Anthropic and OpenAI contracts adds a clause: ‘Within 90 days of California publishing verifier/kill-switch standards, vendor will name its designated verification organization and share the latest kill-switch efficacy attestation.’
stories.audience: Policy, security, and compliance leads at companies deploying frontier models in or from California — and vendors selling into that market.
stories.watch: The two-month expert recommendations, accelerated SB 813/AB 1405 timelines, and whether any other state copies the kill-switch language.

source.title: Office of Governor Gavin Newsom, Executive order to accelerate independent oversight and advance an AI kill switch
source.quote: Advance the creation of a ‘kill switch’ for frontier models, with the efficacy of the switch verified on an ongoing basis by an independent verification organization.

stories.theme: Accenture Faculty embeds inside Anthropic as the first evaluator desk
stories.changed: On 18 September 2026, Anthropic announced a partnership with Accenture’s Faculty unit for independent embedded evaluation of frontier AI — fulfilling a commitment from Amodei’s ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’ essay. Faculty will evaluate and red-team models, run alignment assessments, and test safeguards, with access comparable to an employee: watching models take shape in training, following build/deploy decisions, speaking to staff, assessing operations, verifying safety commitments, identifying blind spots, and reporting incidents. Anthropic and Accenture each expect to invest at least $1 billion over five years; Anthropic will fund Accenture directly for now while pursuing pooled/government funding long-term. The partnership is non-exclusive; Anthropic is also in dialogue with METR and other nonprofits to pilot embedded evaluation on their own funding, and more evaluators are expected in coming weeks. Standards for access and reporting do not yet exist.
stories.matters: External PDF audits become something different when the evaluator sits inside the lab with employee-like access — and the first named partner is a global consultancy enterprises already trust for deployment, not only a safety nonprofit.
stories.imply: Buyers can start asking for the embedded-evaluator name, access scope, and incident-reporting path the way they ask for SOC2 — even while standards are unfinished.
uses: Add to frontier RFPs: named embedded evaluator(s), access comparable to employees?, funding model, and how incidents reach customers.
Treat Accenture’s enterprise-deployment lens as complementary to METR-style research evals — ask for both, not either/or.
Do not confuse ‘embedded’ with ‘outsourced accountability’; Anthropic still says model safety remains its responsibility.
stories.example: A bank’s AI governance committee reviewing Claude Enterprise asks: ‘Which embedded evaluator sits inside Anthropic today, what can they see that we cannot, and will their incident reports reach us under our MSA?’ Procurement holds the renewal until Accenture’s scope letter is attached.
stories.audience: Security, risk, and enterprise AI platform owners who need verifiable third-party eyes inside frontier labs — not another self-attestation PDF.
stories.watch: METR/nonprofit pilot details, the next named evaluator, and whether access/reporting standards get written down.

source.title: Anthropic, Partnering with Accenture on embedded evaluation
source.quote: Unlike today’s external evaluators, embedded evaluators will work inside AI companies, with access comparable to an employee's. That access allows them to watch models take shape in training, follow the decisions that govern how those models are built and deployed, and speak directly to employees.

stories.theme: Claude leads 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D — and zero of it is fully autonomous
stories.changed: On 17 September 2026, Anthropic’s Institute published prototype measurements of the pace of AI development inside the lab. The R&D Automation Index (using Epoch AI’s Automation Levels) reports that as of August 2026 Claude ‘leads’ 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D — completing most of a task end-to-end from a high-level prompt under human supervision (AL4) — while work at or above ‘AI collaborates’ (AL3) exceeds 90%, and Claude is not fully autonomous (AL5) for any measured subset. On Anthropic’s most-used internal agent platform, about 30,000 research and engineering agents ran at once; 100% of their actions passed online monitors before execution, with roughly 0.002% (about 1 in 47,000) blocked. A one-week compute snapshot (13–20 July) put about 6% of AI R&D compute toward safety (about 12% of AI-driven AI R&D compute), under a deliberately conservative definition. Anthropic says it will publish updates regularly and wants third parties to verify.
stories.matters: ‘AI builds AI’ stopped being a slogan and became a vendor-published percentage with a named scale — useful for boards that need a number, not a vibes chart.
stories.imply: Enterprise AI leaders can demand the same three measurements (automation share, agent-monitor coverage/block rate, safety compute share) from any frontier vendor — and treat silence as the story.
uses: Ask OpenAI and Google DeepMind for comparable AL3/AL4/AL5 shares and agent-monitor block rates.
Inside your own shop, pilot an automation-level score on one AI-assisted engineering workflow before trusting ‘leads’-tier claims from vendors.
Pair the 26% figure with the 0% AL5 line in exec briefings so ‘AI builds AI’ does not get oversold.
stories.example: A CTO slide for the board: ‘Anthropic says Claude leads 26% of its model R&D under human supervision; none is fully autonomous; ~1 in 47k agent actions blocked online.’ Action item: require the next OpenAI and Google risk packs to match those three cells or mark ‘not disclosed.’
stories.audience: CTOs, AI platform owners, and boards tracking recursive self-improvement risk and vendor transparency — not just benchmark charts.
stories.watch: The next Index update (does ‘leads’ climb?), third-party verification, and whether rivals publish matching numbers.

source.title: Anthropic Institute, Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development inside frontier labs
source.quote: As of August 2026, Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work. Claude ‘leads’ 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work. The share of work at or above ‘AI collaborates’ is above 90%.

stories.theme: Muse hits Mac: the agent works in your real Files, Mail and Messages
stories.changed: On 17–18 September 2026, Meta shipped Muse for Mac — the first Muse client that completes work on the user’s computer. The agent works across native Files, Messages, Calendar, Notes and Mail; access is opt-in, Full Disk Access is optional, settings can change anytime, and Meta says Muse always asks before sensitive actions such as deleting files or sending messages. Muse launched earlier in September on iOS, Android, web and WhatsApp in the US and topped App Store charts; the Mac app extends that agent onto the desktop where most workplace files live. Powered by Muse Spark (Meta’s agentic model), it arrives amid a race among consumer desktop agents.
stories.matters: Workplace AI stops being a browser tab when the agent can open the spreadsheet and the inbox on the machine — with permission gates that IT can actually describe.
stories.imply: Security teams need a Mac agent policy this month: allowed apps, approval-before-send, and whether Muse belongs on managed laptops at all.
uses: Pilot Muse Mac on a non-production Mac with Mail/Calendar only; keep Messages and Full Disk Access off until the approval prompts are boring.
Update MDM/acceptable-use docs: which desktop agents may request Full Disk Access.
Compare approval-before-sensitive-action behaviour to Claude’s ask-before-action default (Briefing 12).
stories.example: An EA asks Muse on Mac to pull tomorrow’s calendar, draft follow-ups in Mail, and leave them unsent. Every send requires a click; IT reviews the permission sheet before rolling the app to the exec team.
stories.audience: Knowledge workers on Mac and IT/security teams writing the first desktop-agent policy.
stories.watch: Enterprise/MDM controls, encrypted Muse builds Meta has teased, and how often users leave approval prompts on after the first week.

source.title: TechCrunch, Meta’s Muse hits Mac, letting the AI take actions on your computer
source.quote: On the Mac, Muse can interact with your files, messages, calendar, notes, and mail, all within their native applications. … the app will always ask for your approval before it performs sensitive actions, Meta says.
